query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated Q235 steel, the natural heterogeneous surface oxide layer is insufficiently protective against chloride attack. By selectively modifying the near‐surface chemistry to favor enrichment in Cr and Nb, a more uniform and adherent passivating film can form. This enhanced passivation layer will suppress the initiation of pitting and overall corrosion-related degradation in harsh, chloride‐rich environments at both room and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, exhibiting a naturally formed, non-uniform oxide layer with microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: A controlled surface treatment that introduces or enriches trace amounts of chromium (Cr) and niobium (Nb) into the near-surface region of Q235 steel.
generation.conditions: Exposure to chloride-containing aggressive environments at room temperature (approximately 25°C) and at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 60°C) to simulate harsh environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense passivation film on the steel surface that is enriched in Cr and Nb, which mediates the barrier properties of the oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The addition of Cr and Nb modifies the chemistry of the native oxide layer, encouraging the formation of a more stable and coherent passive film. This film is less susceptible to localized breakdown by chloride ions, thereby delaying the onset of pitting and reducing overall corrosion rates. In contrast, untreated Q235 steel forms an irregular oxide film with weak protective qualities.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, treated samples with Cr/Nb enrichment will exhibit lower corrosion rates, higher pitting potentials in electrochemical tests, and more uniform, robust passivation films as verified by surface analysis techniques.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with its natural, heterogeneous oxide layer serving as the reference condition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for Q235 steel exposed to environments with significant chloride content and within the tested temperature range (room temperature to approximately 60°C). It may not extend to conditions where temperature or chloride concentration exceeds these bounds.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effect of Cr/Nb enrichment on passivation film properties and the long-term stability of the film under variable environmental stresses remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set receives a controlled surface treatment designed to enrich the near-surface with Cr and Nb, and the other set is left untreated. Expose both sets to a standardized chloride-rich solution under identical conditions at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (around 60°C). Periodically perform electrochemical testing and surface microscopy over a fixed time period.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization to determine pitting potentials
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to measure corrosion resistance
SEM/EDS to assess the morphology and elemental composition of the surface films
XPS analysis for detailed chemical characterization of the passivation layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr/Nb-enriched treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in passivation film uniformity, higher pitting potentials, and lower corrosion rates compared to the untreated control under both room and elevated temperature conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
In this paper, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating with a thickness of 500 μm on Q235 steel substrate was fabricated by plasma spraying. The microscopic results showed that a new Laves phase is formed in the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating compared to the HEA powder, and elemental segregation occurs between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, while the interdendritic phase enriches with the Cr and Nb. The phase composition change and elemental segregation behavior were mainly due to the faster cooling rate of the plasma spraying technique. At the junction of the coating and the substrate, the HEA coating bonded well to the substrate; in addition, the width of transition zone was merely 2 μm. The microhardness of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was 321 HV0.5, which is significantly higher than that of the substrate. In terms of corrosion resistance, the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating has good corrosion resistance in NaCl solution. Although the corrosion form was pitting corrosion, the pitting potential of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was significantly higher than that of other coatings, which was mainly because of the dense passivation film
